newsitem.title: UK: Leumi sees lift-off in Israeli privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Leumi sees lift-off in Israeli privatisation.

text.p: The pace of privatisation in Israel is poised for take-off with the government preparing to modify a key aspect of its privatisation policy, the country's second largest bank said on Monday.
Eitan Raff, chairman of Bank Leumi, told a London conference the government was planning to alter a practice requiring firms undergoing privatisation to sell a controlling stake first.

"I have indications that they are going to reverse this policy," Raff said. "The policy of selling only to a controlling core will be modified...this is a welcome decision by the prime minister's office."

Citing "zero implementation" in the process of selling off Israel's two biggest banks, Bank Leumi and Bank Hapoalim, he levelled a finger at the requirement for the banks to sell a 20 to 25 percent controlling stake, meaning investors needed to stump up some $500 to $600 million.
"This limits the scope of potential buyers substantially," he said.
But he added Israeli decision-makers from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu down were showing renewed commitment to the privatisation process.
"We are not happy with the pace of privatisation, but all the policy-makers in Israel have and are demonstrating their commitment to privatisation," he said.
Foreign investors have been disappointed by Israel's apparent lethargy in opening its economy to the private sector.
But Netanyahu was elected partly on a privatisation platform and has taken Israel's privatisation authority into his own office in an effort to speed up progress.

Raff said the sluggish implementation so far was due in part to the hyperinflation of the late 1970s and 1980s which absorbed the attention of policymakers, while the stock market crash of 1994 slowed it to a crawl.
Proceeds from privatisation since 1993 totalled only $3 billion, he said.
But looking ahead, the government's plans to sell off the banks and embark on a series of enormous infrastructure projects entailed great potential for profit.
He said the Israeli economy was expected to grow by 3.8 percent in 1996, after a downwards revision from 5.8 percent.
He posted a 4.0 percent GDP growth forecast for 1997.
Analysts are concerned about Israel's trade deficit and its balance of payments, which deterioriated sharply in 1995.
Raff forecast exports of goods and services slowing to 4.0 percent growth in 1996 after an initial 8.0 percent forecast.
But he said Israel was starting to see the benefits of liberalised trade, citing the benefits from free trade agreements with the United States and the European Union.
And he was confident of the government's commitment to developing Israel's market economy.

"In the near future we can expect a greater reliance on market forces as government interference continues to diminish and the privatisation process continues to accelerate," he said. --Caroline Brothers, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
